# Democracy experiment {#sec-gs}

@graham2020democracy ask whether voters punish candidates who violate democratic principles when
party and policy favor them. Respondents chose between two hypothetical state legislative candidates
in up to thirteen matchups. The candidates differed in party, economic and social policy, governance
practices, democratic violations, scandals, and personal traits. This chapter reproduces the paper's
results from the saved fit.

```{r}
#| label: gs-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
gs <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
if (is.null(gs)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit gs_q3.rds; see the installation chapter.")
# a short table of estimates
tab <- function(e, digits = 3) {
  out <- e[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "se", "lower", "upper", "n")]
  out[2:6] <- lapply(out[2:6], round, digits)
  out
}
```

```{r}
#| label: gs-knitr
#| include: false
#| cache: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(pointsize = 11))
```

The book's `_figs-helpers.R` has two helpers: `estimate_each()` runs independent targets in
parallel, with the same results as one `sc_estimate()` call, and `pick()` takes rows by name. The
figures come from the package's plot functions (@sec-plots).

```{r}
#| label: gs-helpers
#| cache: false
#| file: _figs-helpers.R
```

## Data and fit

`sc_example_data("gs")` builds the paper's inputs from the bundled `gs2020` data: 1,605 respondents,
20,657 matchups, and 30 coded features. `y = 1` means the left candidate was chosen. The network
uses sixteen respondent characteristics measured before the tasks. The data also carry the paper's
five folds, each fold's early-stopping respondents, and the grouping variables.

```{r}
#| label: gs-data
x <- sc_example_data("gs")
x
head(x$groups)
```

The groups are party ID (`pid7`, from -3 strong Democrat to 3 strong Republican), party (`party`,
leaners counted as partisans), self-described ideology (`ideology`, all respondents), and `PL`, 1
for the 1,377 partisans and leaners. The co-partisan feature is always zero for the 228 pure
independents, whose choices say nothing about that taste, so quantities about party use `w = "PL"`.

The paper fitted one to four taste factors and chose three. The defaults of `sc_fit()` and
`sc_states()` are the paper's settings. The code below reproduces the saved fit in several hours and
is not run here.

```{r}
#| label: gs-fit
#| eval: false
fit_q <- lapply(1:4, function(q) sc_fit(x, q = q))   # five folds at each rank
sc_select_rank(fit_q)
gs <- sc_states(fit_q[[3]])                           # q = 3; M = 300 designs, 4 responses each
sc_save(gs, file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
```

`sc_select_rank()` gives the paper's rank table:

| Taste factors | Held-out log score | Gain over $q - 1$ | Paired $z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | -7.797 | | |
| 2 | -7.772 | 0.0249 | 2.19 |
| 3 (selected) | -7.739 | 0.0329 | 2.99 |
| 4 | -7.742 | -0.0029 | -0.47 |

The log score is the average log probability of a held-out respondent's whole sequence of choices. A
fourth factor does not improve it, so the rule stops at $q = 3$.

## Mean tastes

`sc_mean()` estimates the average utility of one coded feature, on the logit scale. The co-partisan
mean averages over partisans and leaners, the others over all respondents.

```{r}
#| label: gs-means
fn <- gs$data$data$feature_names
w_of <- function(f) if (f == "diff_respParty") "PL" else NULL
means <- sc_estimate(gs, lapply(fn, function(f) sc_mean(f, f, w = w_of(f))))
labels <- c("Co-partisan", "Economic policy (+1)", "Social policy (+1)",
            "Committee structure", "Legislative staffing", "Legislative procedure",
            "Program evaluation", "Record-keeping", "Legislative schedule",
            "Ban protests", "Ignore courts", "Executive orders", "Gerrymander (2 seats)",
            "Gerrymander (10 seats)", "Prosecute journalists", "Close polling stations",
            "Extramarital affair", "Underpaid taxes", "Female", "Asian", "Black", "Hispanic",
            "Farmer", "Lawyer", "Legislative staffer", "Police officer", "Army veteran",
            "Navy veteran", "Small business owner", "Teacher")
tab(means[c(1:3, 10:18), ])
```

Among partisans and leaners, a co-partisan gains 0.81 units of utility on average. Each step toward
the conservative end of economic policy costs 0.24. The means of the seven violations (`u_`) run
from -0.53 (two-seat gerrymander) to -0.90 (prosecuting journalists), and the two scandals (`v_`)
cost -0.94 (an affair) and -1.18 (underpaid taxes). Conduct is measured against the generic
reference position, a candidate who supports an elected oversight board. `plug_in` is the
cross-fitted value before the score correction (@sec-inference).

## Preference shares

`sc_share()` estimates the share of respondents with a positive taste for a contrast, averaging over
each respondent's fitted normal law. The main figure reports shares for party, the two policy
scales, the seven violations and the two scandals. Each needs its own bounded update (about 15
seconds), so they run in parallel.

```{r}
#| label: gs-shares
fig_features <- fn[c(1:3, 10:18)]
shares <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(fig_features, function(f) sc_share(f, f, w = w_of(f))))
tab(shares, 4)
```

An estimated 82.5% of partisans and leaners prefer a co-partisan (95% interval 79.7% to 84.9%).
Shares favoring a violation are near zero and imprecise: 7.3% for closing polling stations (interval
2.0% to 23.4%) and 0.2% for prosecuting journalists (interval 0 to 1). Such a share depends on the
spread of the taste, which is measured imprecisely because each respondent saw each violation once.

## Fitted distributions

`sc_fitted_law()` gives each held-out respondent's normal law of a taste, with the fitted mean and
the spread implied by the taste factors. The population law is their mixture.

```{r}
#| label: gs-laws
laws <- lapply(fn, function(f) sc_fitted_law(gs, f, w = w_of(f)))
attr(laws[[1]], "summary")
head(laws[[1]])
```

The two figures draw all 30 laws, as in the paper's appendix.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-distributions-1
#| fig-cap: "Fitted tastes: party, policy and governance"
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 9.2
sc_plot_laws(laws[1:15], labels = labels[1:15], means = pick(means, fn[1:15]), layout = "panels")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-distributions-2
#| fig-cap: "Fitted tastes: conduct and background"
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 9.2
sc_plot_laws(laws[16:30], labels = labels[16:30], means = pick(means, fn[16:30]), layout = "panels")
```

Blue curves are fitted values before the score correction. Red marks the corrected mean and its 95%
interval, so the two need not line up. Each panel has its own scales. The reference levels are male,
white and business executive.

## Effects on choices

`sc_ame_switch()` gives the average marginal effect (AME) of switching one attribute of a candidate,
the model's counterpart of the AMCE (@sec-quantities). It takes the raw design attribute, the level
and the reference level. For party, the level is the respondent's own party (1 = Democrat, 2 =
Republican) and the reference the other party, so the switch is undefined for pure independents. A
policy AME switches from position 1 to 4 and divides by three, giving the effect per point. A
conduct AME switches from the generic reference position (`g_boardElect`) to the violation.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ames
ame_target <- function(f) {
  if (f == "diff_respParty") {
    sc_ame_switch(f, "party",
                  level = function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                  ref = function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                  design = "gs", w = "PL")
  } else if (f %in% c("diff_p1_num", "diff_p2_num")) {
    sc_ame_switch(f, sub("^diff_(p[12])_num$", "\\1", f), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3)
  } else {
    sc_ame_switch(f, "dem", f, "g_boardElect", design = "gs")
  }
}
ames <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(fig_features, ame_target))
tab(ames)
```

The regression AMCEs are the coefficients of a linear regression of the choice on all 30 coded
differences, among all respondents (partisans and leaners for party).

```{r}
#| label: gs-amce
dat <- gs$data$data                                    # y: choices; d: coded differences
partisan_rows <- rep(gs$data$groups$PL, dat$T) > 0
amce_all <- coef(lm(dat$y ~ dat$d))[-1]
amce_pl <- coef(lm(dat$y[partisan_rows] ~ dat$d[partisan_rows, ]))[-1]
amce <- setNames(c(amce_pl[1], amce_all[-1]), fn)
round(100 * amce[fig_features], 1)
```

A co-partisan gains 14.0 percentage points of support, and a candidate who prosecutes journalists
loses 16.2. The regression AMCEs are 14.1 and -16.1.

The main figure shows each feature's mean taste (A), fitted distribution (B), share with a positive
taste (C), and AME with the regression AMCE as a grey diamond (D).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-preferences
#| fig-cap: "Preferences and choice effects"
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 5.5
lab <- setNames(labels, fn)
sc_plot_preferences(means, setNames(laws, fn), shares, ames, labels = lab, reference = amce,
                    order = fig_features,
                    xlim = list(A = c(-1.55, 1.05), B = c(-4, 4), D = c(-26, 17)),
                    ticks = list(A = c(-1, 0, 1), B = c(-4, 0, 4), D = c(-20, 0, 15)))
```

Panel B's curves are fitted values before the score correction, scaled to the same height, so their
centers need not match Panel A. In Panel C, a hollow point marks a share whose interval spans at
least 95 points and is not drawn.

`sc_table()` gives the same estimates as a table (@sec-plots):

```{r}
#| label: gs-table
#| results: asis
sc_table("Mean utility" = means, "Share favoring" = shares, "Choice effect" = ames,
         order = fig_features, labels = lab, format = "markdown", n = TRUE)
```

## Compensation shares

The *compensation share* is the share of respondents who prefer a co-partisan with a violation to an
otherwise identical non-co-partisan at the generic reference position. In `sc_share()` the contrast
is the sum of the two features. The paper computes it for the seven violations among liberal,
moderate and conservative partisans and leaners: 21 bounded updates.

```{r}
#| label: gs-comp
g <- gs$data$groups
violations <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn, value = TRUE)
comp <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) for (f in violations)
  comp[[length(comp) + 1]] <- sc_share(paste(ideo, f, sep = "."), c(f, "diff_respParty"),
                                       w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
comp_est <- estimate_each(gs, comp)
tab(comp_est[grepl("journalists", comp_est$name), ])
```

An estimated 33.8% of liberal partisans and leaners and 59.6% of conservative ones prefer the
co-partisan who prosecutes journalists, despite its large mean penalty.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-compensation
#| fig-cap: "Compensation shares"
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
by_ideology <- function(ideo) {       # one group's rows, named by violation
  z <- pick(comp_est, paste(ideo, violations, sep = ".")); z$name <- violations; z
}
sc_plot_estimates(Liberal = by_ideology("lib"), Moderate = by_ideology("mod"),
                  Conservative = by_ideology("con"), labels = lab, scale = 100, xlim = c(0, 100),
                  xlab = "Share preferring co-partisan despite violation (%)",
                  main = "Party advantage offsets the violation")
```

Points are bounded estimates and bars 95% log-odds intervals.

`sc_ratio()` returns $-\tau_j / \tau_p$, the mean prosecution penalty in units of the mean partisan
gain, with a delta-method standard error.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ratio
price <- sc_ratio("journalists penalty / co-partisan gain",
                  sc_mean("journalists, partisans", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", w = "PL"),
                  sc_mean("co-partisan", "diff_respParty", w = "PL"))
tab(sc_estimate(gs, price))
```

The ratio is 1.14 (95% interval 0.91 to 1.37), so on average the two are of similar size.

## Candidate contests

`sc_contest()` estimates the expected share choosing the first candidate in a specified matchup,
with position effects set to zero and task shocks kept. Its contrast is the coded difference between
the two candidates. The paper places a co-partisan, with a clean record or prosecuting journalists,
at each social-policy position (1 most liberal, 4 most conservative) against a non-co-partisan at
position 3, all else equal, among liberal, moderate and conservative partisans and leaners.

```{r}
#| label: gs-contests
e <- function(f) as.numeric(fn %in% f)
contests <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
  d <- e("diff_respParty") + (pos - 3) * e("diff_p2_num")
  if (violation == "journalists") d <- d + e("diff_dem_code_u_journalists")
  contests[[length(contests) + 1]] <- sc_contest(paste(ideo, violation, pos, sep = "."), d,
                                                 w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
}
contest_est <- sc_estimate(gs, contests)
wide <- matrix(round(100 * contest_est$estimate, 1), ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(paste(rep(c("liberal", "moderate", "conservative"), each = 2),
                                     c("clean", "journalists"), sep = ", "),
                               paste("position", 1:4)))
wide
```

At position 2, the co-partisan who prosecutes journalists receives an estimated 49.8% among liberal
partisans and leaners and 52.1% among conservative ones, against 74.2% and 67.7% without the
violation: a cost of about 24 and 16 points. These vote shares include task shocks, so they differ
from the compensation shares.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-contests
#| fig-cap: "Expected support in candidate contests"
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 3.3
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4), 2, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(3, .35))
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) {
  row <- function(v) pick(contest_est, paste(ideo, v, 1:4, sep = "."))
  sc_plot_lines("No violation" = row("clean"), "Prosecutes journalists" = row("journalists"),
                x = 1:4, scale = 100, xlab = "Social policy position",
                ylab = if (ideo == "lib") "Expected vote share (%)" else "",
                main = c(lib = "Liberal", mod = "Moderate", con = "Conservative")[[ideo]], legend = FALSE)
}
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("No violation", "Prosecutes journalists"), col = c(blue, red), lty = 1:2,
       lwd = 1.5, pch = 16, pt.cex = .7, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, cex = .85)
```

Shading gives pointwise 95% log-odds intervals.

## Attribute importance

`sc_importance()` gives each attribute's share of a respondent's utility variation over a stated
menu of levels. The paper uses seven attributes: party, the two four-point policy scales, the
fifteen governance, violation and scandal codes as one attribute, sex, race and profession. A policy
scale has one column, so its menu is `matrix(1:4)`. The shares sum to one and come from one joint
update, about nine minutes per group. They have no intervals: in the paper's simulations such
intervals cover less often than stated. The groups are all partisans and leaners, Democrats, and
Republicans (leaners included).

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance
attrs <- list(party = "diff_respParty", econ = "diff_p1_num", social = "diff_p2_num",
              conduct = grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn, value = TRUE),
              sex = grep("^diff_sex_", fn, value = TRUE),
              race = grep("^diff_race_", fn, value = TRUE),
              profession = grep("^diff_pro_", fn, value = TRUE))
imp_groups <- list(All = "PL", Dem = function(g) g$party == "Dem", Rep = function(g) g$party == "Rep")
imp <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(names(imp_groups), function(k)
  sc_importance(attrs, menus = list(econ = matrix(1:4), social = matrix(1:4)),
                w = imp_groups[[k]], names = paste(k, names(attrs), sep = "."))))
imp[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "n", "status")]
```

The figure groups the components into four: policy (economic and social), party, governance and
conduct, and background (sex, race and profession).

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance-summary
combine <- list(policy = c("econ", "social"), party = "party", governance = "conduct",
                background = c("sex", "race", "profession"))
imp_display <- sapply(names(imp_groups), function(k)
  sapply(combine, function(a) sum(pick(imp, paste(k, a, sep = "."))$estimate)))
round(100 * imp_display, 1)
```

Among all partisans and leaners, policy accounts for 46.5% of utility variation, party 32.9%,
governance and conduct 18.3%, and background 2.3%. Policy outweighs party among Democrats (52.5%
against 29.5%). Among Republicans the two are close (39.7% against 36.7%).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-importance
#| fig-cap: "Attribute importance by party"
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.1
sc_plot_importance("All partisans and leaners" = imp[startsWith(imp$name, "All."), ],
                   Democrat = imp[startsWith(imp$name, "Dem."), ],
                   Republican = imp[startsWith(imp$name, "Rep."), ],
                   combine = combine, colors = c("#333333", blue, red),
                   labels = c(policy = "Policy", party = "Party", governance = "Governance/conduct",
                              background = "Background"))
```

Democrats number 723 and Republicans 654. The shares are point estimates, with equal weights over
each attribute's stated levels, and sum to 100% within each group.

## Decisiveness

`sc_decisiveness()` gives how often exchanging two candidates' levels on one attribute would
reverse the choice, holding the other attributes and the task shock fixed. It averages over the
matchups each respondent saw. The conduct swaps take about twenty minutes.

```{r}
#| label: gs-decisiveness
conduct <- grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn)
action <- grep("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", fn[conduct])
generic <- c(TRUE, grepl("^diff_dem_code_g_", fn[conduct]))   # reference row plus generic codes
dec <- estimate_each(gs, list(
  sc_decisiveness(list(party = "diff_respParty"), pairs = list(party = c(2L, 1L)),
                  names = "party", w = "PL"),
  sc_decisiveness(list(conduct = fn[conduct]), pairs = list(conduct = cbind(1L + action, 1L)),
                  allowed = list(conduct = generic),
                  names = sub("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", "", fn[conduct][action]))))
tab(dec)
```

Exchanging party reverses an estimated 36.1% of choices among partisans and leaners (95% interval
33.8% to 38.4%). Exchanging a candidate who prosecutes journalists with one at the generic
reference position reverses 32.0% (27.3% to 37.1%), the most of the seven violations.

## All paper targets

`gs_targets()` below builds every GS quantity in the paper's main results file: a mean and a share
for each of the 30 features, the compensation shares for seven violations in three ideology groups,
24 contests, the switch AMEs and the ratio. `sc_estimate(gs, gs_targets(gs))` reproduces the paper's
estimates, standard errors and intervals in about 40 minutes in one process, mostly for the bounded
updates of its 51 shares.

```{r}
#| label: gs-full
gs_targets <- function(st) {
  fn <- st$data$data$feature_names; g <- st$data$groups
  e1 <- function(j) as.numeric(seq_along(fn) == j)
  tl <- list(); add <- function(t) tl[[length(tl) + 1L]] <<- t
  for (j in seq_along(fn)) {
    w <- if (j == 1L) "PL" else NULL
    add(sc_mean(paste0(fn[j], ".mean"), fn[j], w)); add(sc_share(paste0(fn[j], ".share"), fn[j], w))
  }
  actions <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn)
  for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) {
    wi <- as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL
    for (j in actions) add(sc_share(paste0("comp.", ideo, ".", fn[j]), c(fn[j], fn[1L]), wi))
    for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
      v <- e1(1L) + (pos - 3) * e1(3L)
      if (violation == "journalists") v <- v + e1(match("diff_dem_code_u_journalists", fn))
      add(sc_contest(paste0("contest.", ideo, ".", violation, ".", pos), v, w = wi))
    }
  }
  jm <- sc_mean("journalists.partisan.mean", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", "PL"); add(jm)
  for (j in c(1:3, actions, grep("^diff_dem_code_v_", fn))) {
    if (j == 1L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "party", function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                        function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]], design = "gs", w = "PL"))
    } else if (j <= 3L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), paste0("p", j - 1L), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3))
    } else {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "dem", fn[j], "g_boardElect", design = "gs"))
    }
  }
  add(sc_ratio("journalists.party.price", jm, sc_mean("diff_respParty.mean", "diff_respParty", "PL")))
  tl
}
```

As above, the policy AMEs are per point of the scale.
